etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English ches, chesse, from Old French eschés, plural of eschec, from Medieval Latin scaccus, from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “king [in chess]”), from Classical Persian شاه (šāh, “shah, king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/).

Compare German Schach and Italian scacchi. Compare French échecs (“chess”) and its descendants: Catalan escacs and Dutch schaak. More at check and shah (“king of Persia or Iran”).

definitions.definition: A board game for two players, each beginning with sixteen chess pieces moving according to fixed rules across a chessboard with the objective to checkmate the opposing king.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Uncertain; perhaps linked to Etymology 1, above, from the sense of being arranged in rows or lines.

definitions.definition: (now chiefly US) Any of several species of grass in the genus Bromus, generally considered weeds.

quote.citation: 2007, Michael Chabon, Gentlemen of the Road, Sceptre, published 2008, page 59:
quote.text: Hobbled, loudly gourmandizing the dry chess grass, they were guarded by a pair of dismounted soldiers in long, dusty coats [...].

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Compare French châssis (“a framework of carpentry”).

definitions.definition: (military, chiefly in the plural) One of the platforms, consisting of two or more planks dowelled together, for the flooring of a temporary military bridge.

quote.citation: 1881, Thomas Wilhelm, A Military Dictionary and Gazetteer:
quote.text: the balks are laid and covered with chesses to within 1 foot of the trestle

quote.citation: 1885, Edward S. Farrow, Farrow's Military Encyclopedia; A Dictionary of Military Knowledge:
quote.text: ach chess consists of three planks.
